content: Dengue is a significant mosquito-borne viral infection that is endemic in many lowand middle-income countries, posing a major public health challenge. Severe dengue is a leading cause of mortality in children. Currently, there is no specific treatment for dengue. However, some observational studies suggest that corticosteroids might be beneficial in managing dengue-related shock, and there is speculation that early administration of corticosteroids could potentially prevent progression to severe illness. The objective of this review was to compare the outcomes of treating dengue with corticosteroids versus placebo or no corticosteroids, specifically focusing on preventing shock-related mortality and disease progression in both children and adults. To gather evidence, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Disease Group Centralized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and LILACS, up to January 6, 2014. Reference lists were screened, and study authors were contacted for additional information when necessary. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared corticosteroids with placebo or no corticosteroids in patients diagnosed with dengue-related shock or in the early symptomatic phase of dengue with positive serology. Two independent researchers screened the records for eligibility, extracted data, and assessed the quality of the studies. The findings were presented in meta-analyses and summary tables, and the quality of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Eight studies involving a total of 948 participants were included in this review. The findings are as follows: 1. Patients with Dengue-Related Shock: Four studies focused on children under 15 years of age with dengue-related shock, conducted in hospitals in Southeast Asia. These studies evaluated the use of intravenous corticosteroids. The trials did not demonstrate any significant effect of corticosteroids on mortality (four trials, 284 participants, very low-quality evidence). There was no observed effect on the need for blood transfusion (two trials, 89 participants, very low-quality evidence), pulmonary hemorrhage (one trial, 63 participants, very low-quality evidence), convulsions (one trial, 63 participants, very low-quality evidence), or the duration of hospitalization (one trial, 63 participants, very low-quality evidence). The evidence base is too limited to definitively confirm or rule out clinically meaningful effects. Additionally, these trials were conducted over 20 years ago and had several methodological limitations. 2. Patients with Early-Stage Dengue: Four studies included 664 children and adults with early-stage dengue (without shock) from Colombia, India, Sri Lanka, and Vietnam. These studies evaluated both oral and intravenous corticosteroids. There was no evidence that corticosteroids reduced mortality (four trials, 664 participants, low-quality evidence). Corticosteroids did not appear to prevent complications of severe dengue, such as shock (two trials, 286 participants, very low-quality evidence), severe bleeding (two trials, 425 participants, very low-quality evidence), severe thrombocytopenia (one trial, 225 participants, very low-quality evidence), ascites (one trial, 178 participants, very low-quality evidence), or the need for intensive care unit (ICU) admission (two trials, 286 participants, very low-quality evidence). Conclusions: The evidence regarding the use of corticosteroids in dengue is inconclusive, with the quality of evidence ranging from low to very low. This applies to both the use of corticosteroids in managing dengue-related shock and in treating early-stage dengue. There is insufficient evidence to determine the effects of corticosteroids in these contexts outside of a randomized controlled trial setting.
